newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Summary of Environment Council Auto/Oil speeches.
newsitem.headline: Summary of Environment Council Auto/Oil speeches.

text.p: The European Parliament is due on Wednesday to hold a public hearing on the European Commission's auto/oil proposals of June 18, 1996.

The hearing follows mixed reactions from environment ministers at their public session in Luxembourg last month and a flurry of papers from the various parties following the fate of auto/oil and its related legislation.
Below is a summary of member states' interventions during the October 15 Environment Council
The Commission proposals are outlined in COM(96)248.
GENERAL REMARKS

Austrian Environment Minister Martin Bartenstein criticised the proposals generally as too focused on cutting nitrogen oxides (NOx) at the expense of cutting carbon dioxide (CO), hydrocarbons (HCs) and benzene emissions.
Belgian Secretary of State for the Environment Jan Peeters said of the proposals in general: "We are highly satisfied with what the Commission has promised us."

Britain, represented by Lord Lindsay, a junior Scottish office minister, was generally in favour of the proposals, saying: "The UK believes the proposals to be ambitious and constitute a technical challenge to industry. The UK would be opposed to any proposal to amend these arbitrarily."
Britain supported the proposals' two-stage approach along with the planned 1998 review prior to any second stage.
Irish deputy minister Liz McManus said the auto/oil proposals were "objective and viable" and a "realistic anticipation of the standards".
"The final outcomes of the two proposals must be implemented at the same time otherwise the dangers of delays and watered down measures are very real," McManus added.

Italian Environment Minister Edo Ronchi said more measures should target cars already on the road because of the slow turnover of car fleets in some countries. He added that with 70 percent of Italian cars operating without catalysts, Rome would have to consider giving incentives for people to renew cars.

A French deputy ambassador said the proposals needed to be supplemented, mentioning vehicle scrapping schemes as an option. He said France accepted the proposals and he agreed with the year 2000 figures set for diesel-engined vehicles.
"I do want to stress that it will be extremely difficult to meet these standards," he said, adding that much more work was needed on a second programme before setting standards for 2005.
FUEL PROPOSALS
Dutch Environment Minister Margreet De Boer, who as the next environment Council president will be in a strong position to influence the proposals, said targets for 2010 were not ambitious enough.

As a general remark about vehicle emissions, she said in reference to Directive 94/12: "We were very very concerned about road traffic emissions but not much has changed since that directive so we have to do our best to limit emissions. We need much stricter, much tougher standards."
"From a health point of view we really cannot consider them at all ambitious," she added.

De Boer said of the diesel and petrol proposals: "I do not think they go sufficiently far. On NOx: "I do not think they are sufficiently tough...It's perfectly possible to go further than what's been proposed."
Finland said the draft suggested weaker rules for fuels than those already in place in several countries.
Danish Environment Minister Svend Auken said he was unhappy with limit values proposed for benzene, sulphur and aromatics.

Italy's Ronchi said: "We do not really understand why benzene and aromatics, which are in fact amongst the most highly polluting elements, are left at such high levels. We have established much lower levels ourselves."

Ferreira said: "We are going to have to look at the question of a transition period to adapt fuels to new standards. It's going to require large investments in order for us to be able to adapt to the standards being proposed."
Ireland also expressed concern about the cost implications of the benzene and sulphur standards.
German Environment Minister Angela Merkel said fuel quality should be uniform in the EU and called for reduction of the proposed sulphur and benzene limits.
"It is important to improve fuel quality because that will also increase the effectiveness of catalytic converters,"
BENZENE IN FUEL

Swedish Environment Minister Anna Lindh said fuel proposals were too weak. "Cleaner fuel makes the catalytic converter work better. We should use the 2000 requirement for better fuel and better technology," she said.
Luxembourg was also in favour of reinforcing fuel limit values, especially for benzene.
Bartenstein said Austria did not want benzene limits to move above a one percent maximum.

Auken said: "We have already agreed with our industry that next year we are going to be down to one percent and we are doing this on the basis of a differentiated tax. We are looking to all our fuels being one percent benzene fuels."
Ireland expressed concern about the cost implications of the benzene and sulphur standards.
SULPHUR IN FUEL
On sulphur Lindh said: "Already there is fuel available on the market with less than a tenth of the levels... the Commission has proposed to tolerate after 2000".
Finland also said proposals did not go far enough on sulphur.

Greek Secretary of State for the Environment Theodoros Koliopanos said with reference to rules on the sulphur content of fuels that international experience showed more significant progress could be made but then added:

"The fuel industry, like any other industry, needs a certain period of time to adjust themselves which means that they need at least a 10-year timetable to work to. Implementation of these very ambitious targets will require serious investment."
Austria wants sulphur in diesel set at 50 parts per million (ppm) not 350 ppm.
LEADED PETROL BAN

On the lead-in-petrol deadline, with its possible two-year deferral to 2002, Koliopanos said: "This deadline is not realistic, not for the conditions in Greece at least. In Greece, about 65 percent of vehicles do not have catalytic converters, they are using old technology...We would like this exemption extended beyond 2002."
Luxembourg said it was particularly in favour of a ban on leaded petrol for the year 2000.
Belgium's Peeters urged that lead in petrol be banned as soon as possible.
Britain supported fiscal instruments for a phase-out of leaded petrol rather than an outright ban.
Ireland's McManus said: "We will have to think carefully about the timing of the ban on leaded fuel."

Spanish Environment Minister Isabel Tocino said her country would ask for a derogation on the marketing of leaded petrol. "We feel that we need a greater time period if we are to realistically comply with this target," she said.
VEHICLES PROPOSALS

Koliopanos said his country wanted more on vehicle maintenance in the vehicles proposal. He said vehicle scrappage incentives would not solve fleet problems on their own and added that the Commission's planned proposals for end-of-life scrap cars should be included in proposals.
Ireland's McManus said there should be more consideration of cold-start tests, in-service compliance and fiscal incentives.
Environment Minister Elisa Ferreira said Portugal was "totally in agreement" with the vehicle emissions proposals, adding that they would demand great efforts to replace old cars.
IN-USE COMPLIANCE TESTS
Italy's Ronchi said in reference to in-use compliance: "If a catalytic converter does not work, it's the manufacturer who must be responsible."
Britain was against the idea of in-use conformity checking.
ON-BOARD DIAGNOSTIC TESTS
Merkel said OBD and in-use compliance were absolutely vital in the discussions.
COLD START

Finland's Pekka Haavisto said the proposals did not take into account cold climates, an issue related to the question of cold start tests for new cars. Sweden's Lindh also favoured cold start tests, as did Austria's Bartenstein, the Netherlands and Denmark.
Bartenstein said alpine conditions created similar emission problems to Arctic ones.
FISCAL INCENTIVES
Sweden said economic incentives were cost effective and a good good way to encourage best available technology.
Finland backed the draft's article on economic incentives.

Britain said fiscal instruments should be allowed for those member states wanting to apply higher standards: "Why should a member state be prohibited for incentivising a diesel engine to meet, for example, the NOx standards quoted for petrol engines? That is unnecessary and undesirable," Lindsay said.

Portugal favours fiscal incentives for new cars along with coordination of related policies such as incentives to use trains and underground systems and to stimulate research into non-traditional fuels.
The French official said a balance was needed between the need to provide incentives for new technologies while avoiding fragmentation of the internal market.
BEST AVAILABLE TECHNOLOGY IN PROPOSALS
"It's rather foolish if the BAT is to be sold in the U.S. but not in Europe," Lindh said.

Auken said: "The Commissioner and others say that we do not need BAT. They are approaching this from a costs viewpoint. In the IPPC directive I thought we had found an appropriate balance between BAT and costs," he said.
